title: Thorium Clocks Start Ticking With Lasers
source_used: Hackaday (article read in full); Nature paper page read for the date and abstract only
key_facts: Researchers at Vienna University claim a thorium-based clock that is self-regulating.
Hackaday says it is not necessarily more accurate than other atomic clocks.
Earlier thorium experiments needed another nuclear clock to supply a laser with precise enough properties.
Here a laser excites a thorium crystal and the crystal's output is used to adjust the laser.
If the laser drifts, the thorium nuclei absorb less light, which corrects the output frequency.
The source paper is in Nature; Hackaday says the research has promise for even more accurate results in the future.
quote_evidence: Researchers at Vienna University claim to have a superior thorium-based atomic clock.
It isn’t necessarily more accurate than other atomic clocks, but it is self-regulating.
If the laser drifts, the thorium nuclei absorb less light, and that adjusts the output frequency to compensate.
why_it_matters_hint: A clock that corrects its own laser needs no second reference clock, a step toward more stable time standards (Hackaday: promise for more accurate results in the future).
event_date: 7 Oct 2026 (Nature online publication, per the Nature page; Hackaday does not give a date)
notes: Hackaday article body is short and calls the device an atomic clock; the Nature page (doi 10.1038/s41586-026-11084-4, online 2026/10/07, 'A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop') calls it a nuclear clock and says it was compared with a Yb+ single-ion clock, with instability approaching 1e-15 over 1 day and several orders of magnitude improvement projected. Reader comments printed under the Hackaday article (nuclear vs atomic clock, 2-3 orders of magnitude) are not article text and were not used as facts. Event is 4 days before the 11 Oct window, so scored as stale.
